triage.name: Atrial Fibrillation
triage.reason: Very common arrhythmia presenting with palpitations, dyspnea or incidentally; diagnosis by ECG with rich teaching on stroke risk and rate/rhythm management.

review_issues: auto-repaired: ecg: dropped extra keys ['leads'] (findings carry their own leads)
presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: Risk rises steadily with age; most patients are over 65
More common in people of European ancestry than in other groups
Men are affected somewhat more often than women

risk_factors.text: Valvular heart disease, especially mitral valve disease
COPD or other chronic lung disease
Recent heart, lung, or esophageal surgery
Stimulant drug use such as cocaine or methamphetamine

family_history: Atrial fibrillation in a parent or sibling
Early heart disease in the family

chief_complaints.text: My heart is racing and fluttering in my chest
I get tired so easily, even just walking to the mailbox
I feel like my heart is skipping beats
I get short of breath when I do anything
I felt lightheaded and almost passed out
My doctor told me my pulse was irregular at my checkup

hpi.onset: Often sudden, over seconds to minutes; sometimes noticed only when a clinician checks the pulse or on a routine ECG
hpi.duration: Episodes may last minutes to hours and stop on their own, or the rhythm may stay irregular for days, weeks, or longer
hpi.progression: Variable: some people have brief episodes that come and go, others have episodes that last longer over time, and some remain in the irregular rhythm continuously
hpi.location: Chest, with the sensation of the heartbeat felt in the chest and sometimes the neck
hpi.quality: Fast, irregular, fluttering or pounding heartbeat; often described as a fish flopping or a drumroll rather than a steady beat
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate for most; can be severe when the rate is very fast or when heart failure or low blood pressure develops
hpi.timing: Episodes can start at any time, often at rest or at night; exercise and alcohol can bring them on
relieving: Episodes may stop on their own

associated_symptoms.text: Shortness of breath when lying flat
Swelling in the ankles or legs
Waking up at night short of breath
Sudden weakness or numbness on one side, trouble speaking, or vision loss (from a clot causing a stroke)

pertinent_negatives: Crushing chest pain that radiates to the arm or jaw and comes on with exertion
Recent long car ride, flight, or leg surgery with one-sided leg swelling
Sudden sharp chest pain that worsens with a deep breath
Known prior heart attack with the same pain

positives.text: Palpitations or fluttering in the chest
Swelling in the legs or ankles

negatives: Pain that radiates to the arm or jaw
Pain brought on reliably by exertion and relieved by rest

positives.text: Shortness of breath when lying flat
Waking at night short of breath
Sudden one-sided weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking

negatives: New confusion or trouble finding words
Loss of vision in one eye

positives.text: Anxiety or worry about the heartbeat

negatives: Panic attacks that reliably precede the palpitations

positives.text: Heat intolerance, tremor, or weight loss

general.mild: Comfortable, no distress; may be unaware of the rhythm
general.moderate: Mildly anxious or restless, aware of the heartbeat
general.severe: Dyspneic at rest or with minimal effort, diaphoretic, prefers sitting upright
general.critical: Ill-appearing, pale and clammy, confused or lethargic, may be hypotensive

findings.maneuver: Palpate the radial pulse for at least 30 seconds (or auscultate the heart)
findings.finding: Irregularly irregular rhythm with a variable rate and pulse deficit relative to the apical rate

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart at the apex and base
findings.finding: Irregularly irregular heart sounds with variable intensity of S1

findings.maneuver: Count the heart rate by auscultation or on the monitor
findings.finding: Heart rate above 100/min

findings.maneuver: Compare the apical rate by auscultation with the radial rate by palpation simultaneously
findings.finding: Radial rate lower than the apical rate

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the apex with the bell while the patient lies on the left side
findings.finding: Third heart sound suggesting heart failure
Crackles at the bases from pulmonary congestion

findings.maneuver: Inspect the internal jugular venous pulsation with the patient at 30–45 degrees
findings.finding: Elevated jugular venous pressure

findings.maneuver: Press over the dorsum of the foot and lower shin for several seconds
findings.finding: Pitting edema of the lower extremities

findings.maneuver: Auscultate all valve areas for murmurs
findings.finding: Murmur suggesting valvular disease, such as mitral stenosis or regurgitation

findings.maneuver: Measure the blood pressure in both arms
findings.finding: Low blood pressure or a narrow pulse pressure

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation and level of alertness
findings.finding: Confusion or lethargy from poor perfusion

findings.maneuver: Perform a focused neurologic exam including strength, speech, and facial symmetry
findings.finding: Focal weakness, sensory loss, or speech difficulty from a cardioembolic stroke
Regular rhythm with a normal rate
No murmur or gallop
Clear breath sounds without crackles or wheezing

labs.caveat: Hyperthyroidism is a reversible cause; check in every new diagnosis. Values shown are for hyperthyroid patients; most patients with AFib have a normal TSH.
Only abnormal when thyrotoxicosis is the driver.
Anemia worsens symptoms and can precipitate AFib; also matters before anticoagulation.
Low platelets affect the choice and safety of anticoagulation.
Kidney function drives anticoagulant dosing and is part of stroke and bleeding risk scores.
Hypokalemia (diuretics) promotes AFib; hyperkalemia can widen the QRS and mimic other rhythms.
Low magnesium makes rate control harder and predisposes to arrhythmia.
Mild elevations are common from demand ischemia with a fast rate; a rising pattern suggests acute coronary syndrome and changes management.
Elevated in heart failure, which is both a cause and a consequence of AFib.
Baseline before starting warfarin; therapeutic range for AFib is usually 2.0–3.0. Normal if the patient is not on warfarin.
Prolonged only if the patient is on heparin or has a coagulopathy.
Diabetes is common and adds to stroke risk.
Not part of AFib workup; only if pulmonary embolism is being considered.

findings.finding: Irregularly irregular ventricular response with no consistent pattern
No discrete P waves; instead a fine, chaotic undulating baseline (fibrillatory waves), best seen in V1
Ventricular rate usually 100–160/min when untreated; may be normal or slow with rate-controlling drugs or conduction disease
Narrow QRS unless there is a bundle branch block or pre-excitation
Coarse or fine fibrillatory activity in V1; R-R intervals vary by more than 10%
Pre-excited AFib: irregular, very fast, wide-complex rhythm with varying QRS width (must-not-miss; avoid AV nodal blockers)
Left ventricular hypertrophy or prior Q waves suggesting hypertensive or ischemic heart disease
QT interval may be prolonged by antiarrhythmic drugs; measure after rate control
ST depression or T-wave inversion from demand ischemia during rapid rates
Complete heart block with a regular slow escape rhythm argues against AFib as the sole rhythm

findings.text: Reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (heart failure)
Mitral stenosis or significant mitral regurgitation
Left atrial thrombus (rare on TTE; better seen on TEE)

imaging.preferred_when: Before cardioversion when the duration of AFib is over 48 hours or unknown, or when anticoagulation has been inadequate

findings.text: Spontaneous echo contrast (smoke) in the left atrium
Pulmonary venous congestion or edema when heart failure is present

imaging.preferred_when: New focal neurologic deficit or altered mental status

findings.text: No acute hemorrhage (allows consideration of anticoagulation)
Hypodense area in a vascular territory consistent with ischemic stroke

imaging.preferred_when: Planning catheter ablation or when echocardiography is inconclusive

findings.text: Left atrial and pulmonary vein anatomy for ablation planning

initial.why: Confirms the diagnosis by showing an irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves
Anemia, infection, or thrombocytopenia affecting anticoagulation
Potassium, magnesium-related electrolytes, and kidney function for drug dosing
Reversible cause; hyperthyroidism must be excluded
Looks for acute coronary syndrome or demand ischemia with rapid rates
Assesses for heart failure as a cause or consequence

initial.only_if: dyspnea, heart failure signs, or suspected pulmonary disease

initial.why: Evaluates chamber size, valves, and ejection fraction; guides anticoagulation and rhythm strategy

confirmatory.why: Captures paroxysmal AFib when the resting ECG is normal
confirmatory.only_if: symptoms are intermittent and the ECG does not show AFib
symptoms occur less than once a day

supporting.why: Rules out left atrial thrombus before cardioversion
supporting.only_if: AFib duration over 48 hours or unknown, or anticoagulation inadequate

supporting.why: Diabetes adds to stroke risk and guides risk factor control
Corrects magnesium before rate or rhythm control

supporting.only_if: new focal neurologic deficit or altered mental status

not_indicated.why: No role in diagnosing AFib; only if pulmonary embolism is suspected
Not needed unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis
No role unless urinary infection is suspected as a trigger
Not indicated for AFib; only if meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage is suspected
Not indicated unless sepsis is suspected as a trigger
Not part of routine workup; reserved for ablation planning

decision_points: Confirm AFib on ECG before starting treatment; if paroxysmal and not captured, use ambulatory monitoring
Check TSH in every new diagnosis to exclude hyperthyroidism
Assess stroke risk with CHA2DS2-VASc and bleeding risk with HAS-BLED before starting anticoagulation
If duration over 48 hours or unknown, anticoagulate for at least 3 weeks or perform TEE before cardioversion
In pre-excited AFib with a wide, fast, irregular rhythm, avoid AV nodal blockers and use electrical cardioversion
Unstable patients (hypotension, ischemia, pulmonary edema, altered mental status) get urgent synchronized cardioversion

criteria.name: CHA2DS2-VASc stroke risk
criteria.summary: Assigns points for heart failure, hypertension, age 75 or older, diabetes, prior stroke or transient ischemic attack, vascular disease, age 65–74, and female sex. Higher scores mean higher yearly stroke risk and support anticoagulation.

criteria.name: HAS-BLED bleeding risk
criteria.summary: Estimates major bleeding risk on anticoagulation using hypertension, abnormal kidney or liver function, stroke, bleeding history, labile INR, age over 65, and drugs or alcohol. High scores prompt closer monitoring rather than withholding anticoagulation.

differential.name: Atrial flutter
differential.why_considered: Also causes a fast, irregular-feeling heartbeat in older patients with the same risk factors, and often coexists with atrial fibrillation.

history: Palpitations that feel rapid and steady rather than chaotic
Often paroxysmal with abrupt onset and offset
exam: Pulse may be regular when the conduction ratio is fixed, or irregular when it varies
ecg: Sawtooth flutter waves at about 300/min, best seen in II, III, aVF and V1
Ventricular rate often close to 150/min (2:1 conduction)
Regular atrial activity rather than a chaotic fibrillatory baseline

differential.name: Multifocal atrial tachycardia
differential.why_considered: Irregular tachycardia in older patients with chronic lung disease, a group that also develops atrial fibrillation.

history: Severe COPD or another chronic lung disease
Recent respiratory infection or theophylline use
exam: Signs of lung disease such as wheezing or prolonged expiration
ecg: Discrete P waves of at least three different morphologies
Rate over 100/min with varying P-P, P-R, and R-R intervals
P waves are present, unlike atrial fibrillation

differential.name: Sinus tachycardia
differential.why_considered: Fast heartbeat with palpitations and dyspnea, and a common response to fever, pain, anemia, or dehydration.

history: Gradual onset and offset rather than sudden
Identifiable trigger such as fever, pain, exercise, or blood loss
exam: Regular pulse and regular heart sounds
Signs of the underlying cause such as fever or pallor
ecg: Regular rhythm with a consistent P wave before every QRS
Rate typically under 150/min and varies with the trigger

differential.name: Supraventricular tachycardia (AV nodal reentrant)
differential.why_considered: Sudden-onset rapid palpitations in a patient without structural heart disease.

history: Abrupt onset and abrupt termination, often with a single triggering event
Younger age and prior similar episodes
ecg: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150–250/min
P waves hidden in or just after the QRS
Regular R-R intervals

differential.name: Ventricular tachycardia
differential.why_considered: Fast rhythm causing palpitations, dyspnea, and hypotension, and can be mistaken for a rapid irregular rhythm on a monitor.
differential.trigger: Wide-complex tachycardia, especially with known coronary disease or heart failure, or any tachycardia with hemodynamic collapse

history: Prior myocardial infarction or cardiomyopathy
Syncope or near-syncope at onset
exam: May be hemodynamically unstable with hypotension or altered mental status
Cannon A waves in the neck from AV dissociation
ecg: Wide QRS over 120 ms with a regular or slightly irregular rhythm
AV dissociation with occasional capture or fusion beats
No fibrillatory baseline

differential.name: Wolff-Parkinson-White with pre-excited atrial fibrillation
differential.why_considered: Irregular, very fast tachycardia that can be fatal if AV nodal blockers are given.
differential.trigger: Irregular wide-complex tachycardia faster than 200/min, especially in a younger patient

history: Prior episodes of rapid palpitations since youth
Family history of sudden cardiac death
exam: Very fast, irregular pulse with hemodynamic compromise
ecg: Irregularly irregular, wide-complex tachycardia with varying QRS width
Delta wave and short PR interval on a baseline ECG in sinus rhythm

differential.name: Atrial fibrillation with aberrancy or bundle branch block
differential.why_considered: Irregular rhythm with wide QRS that can be confused with ventricular tachycardia.

history: Known prior bundle branch block
Similar appearance on prior ECGs
ecg: Irregularly irregular rhythm with a consistent wide QRS morphology
No AV dissociation
Fibrillatory baseline in V1

differential.name: Sick sinus syndrome with tachy-brady episodes
differential.why_considered: Older patients with palpitations alternating with dizziness or syncope, and it frequently coexists with atrial fibrillation.

history: Alternating fast and slow heart rates
Syncope or near-syncope between episodes
ecg: Sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses, or sinoatrial exit block between episodes of tachycardia
P waves present during slow periods

differential.name: Anxiety or panic attack
differential.why_considered: Palpitations, chest discomfort, and breathlessness in a patient with a racing heartbeat.

history: Episodes tied to stress or specific situations
Fear of dying or losing control during episodes
Symptoms resolve with calming
exam: Regular pulse with normal rate between episodes
No pulse deficit or irregular heart sounds
ecg: Normal sinus rhythm
No fibrillatory waves

differential.name: Hyperthyroidism
differential.why_considered: A reversible cause of palpitations, tachycardia, and atrial fibrillation itself.

history: Heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor, diarrhea
Neck swelling or prior thyroid disease
exam: Diffuse goiter, tremor, warm moist skin, lid lag
labs: Low TSH with elevated free T4 or T3

severity.mild: Paroxysmal or persistent AFib with a controlled rate, no or minimal symptoms, hemodynamically stable, no heart failure
severity.moderate: Symptomatic with fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, or palpitations; rate 90–140/min; may have mild pulmonary congestion or lower extremity edema
severity.severe: Rapid ventricular response 120–170/min with dyspnea at rest, pulmonary crackles, elevated JVP, hypotension, or new heart failure decompensation
severity.critical: Hemodynamic instability with hypotension, altered mental status, shock, pulmonary edema, or acute coronary ischemia; also includes pre-excited AFib with a very fast wide-complex rhythm

red_flags.finding: Hypotension or systolic blood pressure under 90 mmHg
red_flags.meaning: Poor perfusion from the rapid rate; needs urgent synchronized cardioversion
Cerebral hypoperfusion or embolic stroke; urgent evaluation

red_flags.finding: Chest pain with ST changes on ECG
red_flags.meaning: Demand ischemia or acute coronary syndrome; urgent cardiology involvement

red_flags.finding: Acute pulmonary edema with crackles and hypoxia
red_flags.meaning: Rate-related heart failure; needs urgent rate control or cardioversion
Pre-excited AFib; avoid AV nodal blockers and cardiovert

red_flags.finding: New focal neurologic deficit or speech difficulty
red_flags.meaning: Cardioembolic stroke; activate stroke pathway and obtain urgent head imaging
Severe hypoperfusion or another arrhythmia such as ventricular tachycardia

complications.name: Cardioembolic stroke
clues: Sudden focal weakness, numbness, or speech difficulty
No anticoagulation or subtherapeutic anticoagulation
High CHA2DS2-VASc score

complications.name: Heart failure from tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy
clues: Weeks to months of uncontrolled rapid rates
Progressive dyspnea, edema, and reduced ejection fraction
Improves with rate or rhythm control

complications.name: Systemic arterial embolism
clues: Sudden limb pain, pallor, or pulselessness
Acute abdominal pain from mesenteric ischemia
Left atrial thrombus on echocardiography

complications.name: Acute decompensated heart failure
clues: Rapid ventricular rate with crackles, orthopnea, and elevated JVP
Hypoxia and increased work of breathing

complications.name: Sudden cardiac arrest
clues: Collapse with no pulse
Pre-excited AFib degenerating to ventricular fibrillation
Severe underlying structural heart disease

complications.name: Bleeding from anticoagulation
clues: Melena, hematuria, or unexplained bruising
High HAS-BLED score
Supratherapeutic INR or recent NSAID use

complications.name: Cognitive impairment and dementia
clues: Progressive memory difficulty over years
Silent cerebral infarcts on imaging
Long-standing or inadequately treated AFib

special_populations.differences: Often present with fatigue, falls, or confusion rather than palpitations; higher stroke risk and higher bleeding risk, so anticoagulation decisions need careful weighing.

AFib is uncommon in pregnancy; when present, evaluate for structural heart disease and hyperthyroidism. Rate control and anticoagulation choices must account for fetal safety, and anticoagulation is usually with heparin rather than warfarin.

Kidney function determines dosing of anticoagulants such as apixaban, rivaroxaban, and dabigatran; direct oral anticoagulants may be contraindicated in advanced kidney disease, and warfarin may be preferred.
Coagulopathy and impaired drug metabolism increase bleeding risk; anticoagulant choice and dose need adjustment, and HAS-BLED scores are higher.
Obesity is a modifiable risk factor; weight loss reduces AFib burden. Direct oral anticoagulant dosing may need adjustment at higher body weights.
Diabetes adds to stroke risk and is part of the CHA2DS2-VASc score; glucose control is part of overall risk reduction.
AFib is rare in children and usually occurs with congenital heart disease, after cardiac surgery, or with hyperthyroidism; management focuses on the underlying cause.

key_questions.question: What does the racing or fluttering feel like, and did it start suddenly?
key_questions.looking_for: Fast, chaotic, fluttering or pounding heartbeat with abrupt onset, unlike a steady rapid beat

key_questions.question: When did this episode start, and how long has it lasted?
key_questions.looking_for: Duration matters: over 48 hours or unknown duration changes cardioversion planning

key_questions.question: Has this happened before, and how did those episodes end?
key_questions.looking_for: Paroxysmal pattern that stops on its own versus persistent rhythm; prior episodes and prior cardioversions

key_questions.question: What were you doing when it started?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset at rest or at night is typical; exertion or alcohol as a trigger

key_questions.question: How much alcohol do you drink, and how often?
key_questions.looking_for: Heavy or binge drinking is a strong, modifiable trigger

key_questions.question: Do you use cocaine, methamphetamine, or other stimulants?
key_questions.looking_for: Stimulant use as a precipitant

key_questions.question: Do you have chest pain, and is it pressure that comes with exertion?
key_questions.looking_for: Exertional pressure radiating to arm or jaw suggests ischemia rather than AFib alone

key_questions.question: Have you fainted or nearly fainted?
key_questions.looking_for: Syncope or near-syncope suggests severe hypoperfusion or another arrhythmia

key_questions.question: Any sudden weakness on one side, trouble speaking, or vision loss?
key_questions.looking_for: Cardioembolic stroke; activates the stroke pathway

key_questions.question: Are you more short of breath lying flat, or do you wake up at night gasping?
key_questions.looking_for: Orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea suggests heart failure

key_questions.question: Have your ankles or legs been swelling?
key_questions.looking_for: Volume overload from heart failure

key_questions.question: How is your energy level compared with a few months ago?
key_questions.looking_for: Fatigue is the most common symptom and may be the only one

key_questions.question: Do you have high blood pressure, heart failure, valve disease, diabetes, or sleep apnea?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions that cause AFib and add to stroke risk

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a stroke, TIA, or a blood clot?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior stroke or TIA strongly raises stroke risk and pushes toward anticoagulation

key_questions.question: Have you had heart, lung, or esophageal surgery recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent cardiothoracic surgery is a common trigger in the early postoperative weeks

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, including over-the-counter ones?
key_questions.looking_for: Thyroid hormone, albuterol, pseudoephedrine, and diuretics that lower potassium or magnesium

key_questions.question: Do you take any blood thinners, aspirin, or NSAIDs?
key_questions.looking_for: Current anticoagulation status and bleeding risk before starting therapy

key_questions.question: Have you ever had bleeding problems, ulcers, or a fall with a head injury?
key_questions.looking_for: Bleeding history that affects anticoagulant choice

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have atrial fibrillation or early heart disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of AFib or early heart disease

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, and have you ever smoked?
key_questions.looking_for: Tobacco use as a vascular risk factor

key_questions.question: Any fever, cough, or recent infection?
key_questions.looking_for: Acute illness or infection as a precipitant

reasoning_points: Palpitations with an irregularly irregular pulse and variable heart sounds
ECG shows no discrete P waves with a chaotic fibrillatory baseline and irregular R-R intervals
Symptoms of fatigue, exertional dyspnea, or lightheadedness consistent with loss of atrial kick
Risk factors such as age over 65, hypertension, heart failure, or valvular disease
Hyperthyroidism excluded with TSH as a reversible cause
Stroke risk assessed with CHA2DS2-VASc and bleeding risk with HAS-BLED before anticoagulation
Hemodynamic stability assessed; instability requires urgent synchronized cardioversion
Duration over 48 hours or unknown requires anticoagulation or TEE before cardioversion

Irregularly irregular pulse with a pulse deficit
ECG with no P waves and chaotic baseline
Symptoms of fatigue and exertional dyspnea
medium: Paroxysmal AFib with a normal ECG in the office; needs ambulatory monitoring
Patient presenting with fatigue or falls rather than palpitations
AFib with a controlled rate and few symptoms found incidentally
